4. Superior Pulmonary Vein (often anterior to artery)4. Inferior Pulmonary Vein (most inferior)
5. Inferior Pulmonary Vein (most inferior, anterior)
Bronchus positionEparterial and HyparterialOnly Hyparterial (relative to the pulmonary artery)
Overall BulkWider and more vertical (due to early branching of right main bronchus into superior lobar/eparterial bronchus)Narrower and more horizontal
Mnemonic"SEAI" (Superior Bronchus, Artery, Inferior Bronchus, Inferior Vein)"A-B-V" (Artery, Bronchus, Veins) for the main structures, or more precisely the listed order above

Relations of the Root of the Lung

The structures in the mediastinum immediately adjacent to the roots of the lungs are:

* Anterior Relations:

* Phrenic Nerve

* Pericardiacophrenic vessels

* Part of the Mediastinal Pleura

* Cardiac impressions

* Posterior Relations:

* Vagus Nerve (contributing to the pulmonary plexus)

* Descending Thoracic Aorta (Left side only)

* Azygos Vein (Arching over the right root only)

* Esophagus (Right side, slightly posterior)

* Superior Relations:

* Right Root: Arch of Azygos Vein, Right Vagus Nerve, Trachea, Superior Vena Cava.

* Left Root: Arch of Aorta, Left Vagus Nerve, Left Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve.

* Inferior Relations:

* The Pulmonary Ligament, which extends downwards from the hilum, providing a dead space for expansion of pulmonary veins.

Clinical Correlates

* Hilar Lymphadenopathy: Enlargement of the bronchopulmonary lymph nodes within the hilum is a common finding on chest X-rays, indicating conditions such as infections (e.g., tuberculosis), inflammatory diseases (e.g., sarcoidosis), or malignancy (e.g., lung cancer, lymphoma).

* Bronchoscopy and Surgery: A thorough understanding of the anatomical arrangement within the hilum, especially the position of the eparterial bronchus on the right side, is crucial for endoscopic procedures like bronchoscopy and for lung resections (lobectomy, pneumonectomy) to avoid vital structure damage.

1. Describe the formation, branches, distribution and applied anatomy of median nerve. — Repeated 1 time

The median nerve is a major nerve of the upper limb, often referred to as the "laborer's nerve" due to its extensive supply to the flexor muscles of the forearm and hand.

Formation

The median nerve is formed in the axilla by the union of two roots:

  • Lateral root: Arises from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus (C5, C6, C7 spinal segments).
  • Medial root: Arises from the medial cord of the brachial plexus (C8, T1 spinal segments).

These two roots unite in front of the third part of the axillary artery to form a prominent "M" shape, characteristic of the brachial plexus. Its primary spinal segmental representation is C5, C6, C7, C8, T1.

Course

  1. In the Arm: It descends vertically, first lying lateral to the brachial artery in the upper arm, then crossing anterior to the artery to lie medial to it in the lower part of the arm. It gives off no branches in the arm.
  2. In the Cubital Fossa: It passes anterior to the brachialis muscle and posterior to the bicipital aponeurosis. It then enters the forearm between the two heads of the pronator teres muscle.
  3. In the Forearm: It descends between the superficial and deep groups of forearm flexors. Specifically, it lies between the flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) and flexor digitorum profundus (FDP). About 5 cm proximal to the flexor retinaculum, it becomes superficial, lying between the tendons of flexor carpi radialis (FCR) and palmaris longus.
  4. At the Wrist: It enters the palm by passing through the carpal tunnel, deep to the flexor retinaculum. It is the most superficial structure within the carpal tunnel.
  5. In the Hand: Immediately after exiting the carpal tunnel, it divides into its terminal branches.

Branches and Distribution

The median nerve gives off branches only in the forearm and hand.

1. In the Forearm:

  • Muscular Branches: Supply most muscles of the superficial and intermediate flexor compartments of the forearm:
  • Pronator teres
  • Flexor carpi radialis
  • Palmaris longus
  • Flexor digitorum superficialis
  • Anterior Interosseous Nerve (AIN): A purely motor nerve that arises from the posterior aspect of the median nerve in the upper forearm. It supplies:
  • Flexor pollicis longus (FPL)
  • Lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) (supplying index and middle fingers)
  • Pronator quadratus
  • It also provides sensory innervation to the wrist joint and interosseous membrane.
  • Palmar Cutaneous Branch: Arises from the median nerve in the lower forearm, roughly 5 cm proximal to the flexor retinaculum. It passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum to supply sensation to the lateral half of the palm (thenar eminence). Crucially, this branch does not pass through the carpal tunnel.

2. In the Hand:

  • Recurrent Motor Branch (Thenar Motor Branch): A crucial branch that turns sharply back towards the thenar eminence. It supplies the three thenar muscles responsible for thumb movements:
  • Abductor pollicis brevis (APB)
  • Flexor pollicis brevis (FPB) (superficial head)
  • Opponens pollicis (OP)
  • Palmar Digital Branches (Common and Proper): These are terminal sensory and motor branches:
  • Motor: Supply the first and second lumbricals.
  • Sensory: Supply the palmar aspect of the lateral 3½ digits (thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of the ring finger), the distal dorsum and nail beds of these digits.

Applied Anatomy

Injuries to the median nerve result in distinct clinical syndromes depending on the level of the lesion.

  1. High Median Nerve Injury (above the elbow):
  • Motor Loss:
  • Inability to pronate the forearm (due to paralysis of pronator teres and pronator quadratus).
  • Weakness in wrist flexion (FCR).
  • Inability to flex the thumb (FPL), index finger, and middle finger (FDP, FDS).
  • Paralysis of thenar muscles and first two lumbricals.
  • Results in "Ape Thumb Deformity" (thumb adducted and extended, due to paralysis of thenar muscles and unopposed action of adductor pollicis and EPL) and inability to oppose the thumb.
  • Upon attempting to make a fist, the index and middle fingers remain extended, leading to "Pointing Index" or "Oschner's Hand".
  • Sensory Loss: Affects the palmar aspect of the lateral 3½ digits and the corresponding palm, as well as the distal dorsal aspects and nail beds of these digits.
  1. Anterior Interosseous Nerve Syndrome:
  • Lesion of the AIN (e.g., due to compression) leads to weakness or paralysis of FPL, lateral FDP, and pronator quadratus.
  • Patient cannot make an "OK sign" (attempting to oppose thumb and index finger forms a triangle instead of a circle, due to inability to flex DIP of thumb and index finger). This is a classic diagnostic sign.
  • No sensory loss as AIN is a purely motor nerve (except joint sensation).
  1. Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS):
  • Most common median nerve entrapment neuropathy. It results from compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel, often due to inflammation of flexor tendons, overuse, or systemic conditions (e.g., hypothyroidism, pregnancy, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis).
  • Sensory Symptoms: Numbness, tingling, or burning sensation (paresthesia) in the lateral 3½ digits. Symptoms are often worse at night or with repetitive hand movements. The palmar cutaneous branch is usually spared, so sensation over the thenar eminence remains intact.
  • Motor Symptoms: Weakness and atrophy of the thenar muscles (Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis, Opponens pollicis), leading to Ape Thumb Deformity in chronic cases and difficulty with fine motor tasks involving the thumb (e.g., buttoning a shirt).
  • Special Tests: Tinel's sign (tapping over the median nerve at the wrist elicits tingling) and Phalen's maneuver (forced wrist flexion for 60 seconds elicits symptoms) are positive.
  1. Pronator Teres Syndrome:
  • Less common compression of the median nerve as it passes between the two heads of the pronator teres muscle.
  • Symptoms are similar to CTS but often include pain and tenderness in the proximal forearm. It typically affects the palmar cutaneous branch as well, so there may be sensory loss over the thenar eminence. Weakness of all median innervated muscles distal to the site of compression will be present, including those supplied by AIN.
2. Describe the origin, course, relations and distribution of the ulnar nerve. Add a note on its applied anatomy (related to its damage in forearm). — Repeated 1 time

Introduction

The ulnar nerve is one of the two major terminal branches of the medial cord of the brachial plexus, primarily responsible for the innervation of most intrinsic muscles of the hand and sensation to the medial aspect of the hand and digits. It is often referred to as the "musician's nerve" due to its role in fine motor control of the hand.

Origin

The ulnar nerve originates from the medial cord of the brachial plexus. This cord is formed by the anterior divisions of the ventral rami of spinal nerves C8 and T1. Occasionally, it may also receive contributions from C7.

Course and Relations

  1. In the Arm:

* It descends along the medial aspect of the arm, initially lying medial to the axillary artery, then medial to the brachial artery until the mid-arm.

* Around the middle of the arm, it pierces the medial intermuscular septum and passes from the anterior to the posterior compartment.

* It then descends along the posterior aspect of the medial intermuscular septum, lying posterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus. Here, it passes through a fibro-osseous tunnel known as the cubital tunnel (or ulnar groove), where it is vulnerable to compression and injury.

  1. In the Forearm:

* The ulnar nerve enters the forearm by passing between the two heads (humeral and ulnar) of the flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) muscle.

* It then courses distally, lying deep to the FCU and superficial to the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) muscle.

* Throughout its course in the forearm, it is accompanied by the ulnar artery, which lies lateral to the nerve.

* In the distal third of the forearm, it becomes more superficial and lies on the lateral side of the FCU tendon, medial to the ulnar artery.

* Branches in the Forearm:

* Muscular branches: Supply the entire FCU and the medial half of the FDP (to the ring and little fingers).

* Palmar cutaneous branch: Arises in the mid-forearm, runs distally, and supplies sensation to the skin over the hypothenar eminence and medial palm.

* Dorsal cutaneous branch: Arises about 5-8 cm proximal to the wrist, passes dorsally deep to FCU, and supplies the medial third of the dorsum of the hand, the dorsal surface of the little finger, and the medial half of the dorsal surface of the ring finger.

  1. At the Wrist and Hand:

* At the wrist, the ulnar nerve passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum within a fibro-osseous tunnel called Guyon's canal (ulnar canal), located between the pisiform bone medially and the hook of the hamate laterally. Here it lies just lateral to the pisiform bone and medial to the ulnar artery.

* Within Guyon's canal, it terminates by dividing into two main branches:

* Superficial terminal branch: Primarily sensory, supplies the palmar surface of the little finger and the medial half of the ring finger. It also supplies the palmaris brevis muscle.

* Deep terminal branch: Primarily motor, it hooks around the hook of the hamate and travels with the deep palmar arch.

Distribution

  1. Motor Distribution:

* In the Forearm:

* Flexor Carpi Ulnaris (FCU).

* Medial half of Flexor Digitorum Profundus (FDP) (to ring and little fingers).

* In the Hand (via deep terminal branch):

* Hypothenar muscles: Abductor digiti minimi, Flexor digiti minimi brevis, Opponens digiti minimi.

* Lumbricals: Medial two (3rd and 4th).

* All Palmar interossei (3 muscles).

* All Dorsal interossei (4 muscles).

* Adductor Pollicis.

* Deep head of Flexor Pollicis Brevis.

* Palmaris Brevis (via superficial terminal branch).

  1. Sensory Distribution:

* Palmar aspect: Medial one-third of the palm, palmar surface of the little finger, and the medial half of the palmar surface of the ring finger (via palmar cutaneous and superficial terminal branches).

* Dorsal aspect: Medial one-third of the dorsum of the hand, dorsal surface of the little finger, and the medial half of the dorsal surface of the ring finger (via dorsal cutaneous branch).

Applied Anatomy: Damage in the Forearm

Damage to the ulnar nerve in the forearm typically occurs due to deep lacerations, penetrating injuries, or fractures of the distal ulna. The clinical presentation depends on the level of injury.

Clinical Features of Ulnar Nerve Damage in the Forearm:

  1. Motor Deficits:

* Weakness of Wrist Flexion: The Flexor Carpi Ulnaris (FCU) is paralyzed, leading to weakened wrist flexion. The hand also deviates radially during flexion due to unopposed action of the Flexor Carpi Radialis (median nerve).

* Loss of DIP Joint Flexion: Paralysis of the medial half of Flexor Digitorum Profundus (FDP) results in inability to flex the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints of the ring and little fingers.

* Intrinsic Hand Muscle Paralysis:

* Wasting: Significant atrophy of interossei muscles (guttering between metacarpals) and the hypothenar eminence.

* "Ulnar Claw Hand": Hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and flexion at the interphalangeal (IP) joints of the ring and little fingers. This is due to unopposed action of the extensor digitorum and preserved FDP (if lesion is distal to its innervation), coupled with paralysis of the interossei and lumbricals (which normally flex the MCP and extend the IP joints). If the lesion is in the forearm, the FDP to the ring and little fingers is also paralyzed, leading to a less pronounced claw, sometimes called a "partial claw" or "ulnar paradox."

* Froment's Sign: Weakness of Adductor Pollicis. When asked to hold a piece of paper between the thumb and index finger, the patient compensates by flexing the IP joint of the thumb using the Flexor Pollicis Longus (median nerve), causing the thumb pulp to appear concave.

* Card Test: Inability to firmly hold a card between adjacent fingers due to paralysis of the interossei.

  1. Sensory Deficits:

* Loss of sensation over the entire ulnar nerve sensory distribution: the medial one-third of the palm and dorsum of the hand, the palmar and dorsal aspects of the little finger, and the medial half of the palmar and dorsal aspects of the ring finger. This is because the palmar and dorsal cutaneous branches arise in the forearm and would be affected.

The precise location of the injury within the forearm can differentiate symptoms, for example, a lesion proximal to the origin of the dorsal cutaneous branch would involve both palmar and dorsal sensory loss, while a more distal injury near the wrist might spare the dorsal cutaneous supply if it arises proximal to the point of damage.

1. Root value and muscles supplied by the radial nerve. — Repeated 1 time

Root Value

The radial nerve arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus, encompassing root values of C5, C6, C7, C8, T1.

Muscles Supplied

It innervates the following muscles:

  • Arm: Triceps brachii (all heads), Anconeus.
  • Forearm:
  • Superficial Extensor Compartment: Brachioradialis, Extensor Carpi Radialis Longus, Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis, Extensor Digitorum, Extensor Digiti Minimi, Extensor Carpi Ulnaris.
  • Deep Extensor Compartment (via Posterior Interosseous Nerve): Supinator, Abductor Pollicis Longus, Extensor Pollicis Brevis, Extensor Pollicis Longus, Extensor Indicis.

1. Bursa and its functions.

Definition

A bursa (plural: bursae) is a small, flattened sac-like structure lined by a synovial membrane and containing a thin film of viscous synovial fluid. Bursae are strategically located at sites of potential friction in the musculoskeletal system.

Structure

A bursa consists of:

* An outer fibrous layer that is thin but durable, providing structural integrity.

* An inner synovial membrane (synovium) which is responsible for secreting and absorbing the synovial fluid.

* A potential space or cavity containing a small amount of synovial fluid, which acts as a lubricant.

Functions

The primary functions of a bursa are:

  1. Friction Reduction: They act as cushions between structures that move relative to one another, such as bone, muscle, tendons, and skin. This minimizes wear and tear.
  2. Cushioning: They absorb shock and protect underlying tissues from pressure, particularly over bony prominences.
  3. Facilitating Movement: By reducing friction, bursae ensure that movement of tendons and muscles is smooth and effortless.

Types of Bursae

Bursae can be classified based on their location:

* Subcutaneous Bursae: Located between the skin and underlying bony prominences.

* Example: Prepatellar bursa (anterior to the patella) and Olecranon bursa (at the point of the elbow).

* Subtendinous Bursae: Positioned between tendons and bone.

* Example: Retrocalcaneal bursa (between the Achilles tendon and the calcaneus).

* Submuscular Bursae: Found between muscles or between a muscle and an underlying bone or joint capsule.

* Example: Subacromial bursa (between the deltoid muscle/acromion and the supraspinatus tendon/humeral head).

* Adventitious Bursae: These are not always present but may develop in response to abnormal and repeated friction or pressure, often over a bony spur.

Clinical Correlation: Bursitis

Bursitis is the inflammation of a bursa, leading to pain, swelling, and tenderness. The bursa becomes distended with excess fluid.

* Causes:

* Trauma: A direct blow to the area.

* Repetitive Pressure/Friction: Chronic overuse, as seen in certain occupations or sports.

* Infection: Bacteria entering the bursa, often through a skin wound (septic bursitis).

* Systemic Disease: Conditions like rheumatoid arthritis or gout can cause inflammatory bursitis.

* Common Examples:

* Olecranon Bursitis ("Student's Elbow"): Inflammation of the bursa over the olecranon process, often due to prolonged pressure from leaning on elbows.

* Prepatellar Bursitis ("Housemaid's Knee"): Inflammation of the bursa in front of the kneecap, caused by frequent kneeling.

* Subacromial Bursitis: A common cause of shoulder pain, often associated with rotator cuff impingement.

2. What is the difference between a multipennate muscle and a strap muscle?

Multipennate and strap muscles represent distinct classifications based on their fiber arrangement, leading to significant differences in their functional characteristics.

FeatureMultipennate MuscleStrap Muscle
Fiber ArrangementMuscle fibers attach obliquely to multiple tendons.Muscle fibers are long, slender, and run parallel to the long axis.
AppearanceGives a feather-like appearance.Ribbon-like in shape.
Force ProductionDesigned for high force production due to a large number of short fibers.Generates less force per unit area compared to pennate muscles.
Range of MotionHas limited range of motion and typically slower contraction speed.Provides a large range of motion and relatively faster contraction speed.
ExamplesDeltoid, Gastrocnemius.Sartorius, Sternohyoid.

These distinct structural arrangements dictate the mechanical advantages and roles each muscle type plays in generating movement.

3. Give any two examples of pennate muscles with one example of each.

Pennate muscles are those in which the fascicles attach obliquely (at an angle) to a central tendon, resembling a feather. This arrangement allows for a higher density of muscle fibers and greater force production compared to parallel-fibered muscles.

Two types of pennate muscles are:

1. Bipennate Muscle

In a bipennate muscle, the fibers are arranged on both sides of a central tendon. This structure is very similar to that of a typical feather.

* Example: Rectus femoris, one of the quadriceps muscles in the thigh.

2. Multipennate Muscle

In a multipennate muscle, the fibers attach obliquely to multiple tendons that branch within the muscle, giving it a complex, feather-like appearance. This design is suited for high force production.

* Example: Deltoid muscle of the shoulder.

4. Bipennate muscle.

Definition

A bipennate muscle is a type of pennate muscle where muscle fibers are arranged obliquely on both sides of a central tendon, resembling a feather. This arrangement allows for a large number of muscle fibers to be packed into a small area.

Characteristics

* Fiber Arrangement: Muscle fibers run at an angle to the central tendon, attaching obliquely to it from two directions.

* Force Production: Like other pennate muscles, bipennate muscles are designed for high force production. This is due to their large physiological cross-sectional area (PCSA), which results from packing numerous short fibers into a given volume.

* Range of Motion: They typically exhibit a limited range of motion compared to muscles with parallel fiber arrangements (e.g., strap muscles).

* Contraction Speed: Contraction speed is generally slower than strap muscles, but the force generated is significantly greater.

* Mechanical Advantage: The oblique arrangement allows for a greater number of sarcomeres in parallel, optimizing force generation at the expense of individual fiber length and speed.

Examples

* Rectus Femoris: A large quadriceps muscle that extends the knee and flexes the hip.

* Gastrocnemius: Part of the calf muscle, responsible for plantarflexion of the foot (though the source classifies it as multipennate, its medial and lateral heads are bipennate).

* Flexor Hallucis Longus: A muscle in the posterior leg responsible for flexing the big toe.

* Deltoid: Although primarily classified as multipennate in the source, it contains bipennate sections, particularly the anterior and posterior parts.

5. Prime movers with examples.

Prime Mover (Agonist)

An agonist, also known as a prime mover, is the principal muscle or muscle group that is directly responsible for producing a specific movement. During the action, the prime mover contracts concentrically to generate the necessary force. While prime movers are the main drivers of an action, they operate as part of a coordinated action involving other muscle groups like antagonists and synergists to ensure smooth and controlled movement.

Examples of Prime Movers

Below are key examples of prime movers and the specific movements they produce:

* Elbow Flexion: The Biceps brachii acts as the prime mover, contracting to bend the elbow.

* Knee Extension: The Quadriceps femoris muscle group is the prime mover responsible for straightening the leg at the knee joint.

* Plantarflexion of the Foot: The Gastrocnemius and Soleus muscles in the calf act as the prime movers for pointing the toes downwards, as in standing on tiptoes.

* Shoulder Abduction: The Deltoid muscle is the prime mover for lifting the arm away from the side of the body after the initial 15 degrees.

1. Draw and label a typical spinal nerve. What is its distribution and applied anatomy?

Formation and Structure of a Typical Spinal Nerve

A typical spinal nerve is a mixed nerve, carrying both motor and sensory information. It is formed by the union of dorsal and ventral roots and is a key component of the Peripheral Nervous System (PNS). There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves.

The formation can be visualized as a sequence starting from the spinal cord:

  1. Rootlets: Nerve fibers emerge from the spinal cord as small bundles called rootlets.

* Ventral (Anterior) Rootlets: Arise from the anterolateral sulcus. They contain efferent (motor) fibers whose cell bodies are located in the anterior (ventral) horn of the spinal cord's gray matter.

* Dorsal (Posterior) Rootlets: Enter the spinal cord at the posterolateral sulcus. They contain afferent (sensory) fibers whose cell bodies are located in the dorsal root ganglion.

  1. Roots: The rootlets coalesce to form two major roots.

* Ventral (Anterior) Root: Formed by the union of ventral rootlets. It is purely motor.

* Dorsal (Posterior) Root: Formed by the union of dorsal rootlets. It is purely sensory. It is characterized by a swelling called the Dorsal Root Ganglion (DRG), which contains the cell bodies of the sensory neurons (pseudounipolar neurons).

  1. Spinal Nerve Trunk: The dorsal and ventral roots unite within or just distal to the intervertebral foramen to form the spinal nerve trunk. Because it is formed from the fusion of a sensory and a motor root, the spinal nerve itself is a mixed nerve. This trunk is very short (1-2 cm).

*(Mnemonic: SAME DAVE - Sensory Afferent Motor Efferent; Dorsal Afferent Ventral Efferent)*

Distribution of a Spinal Nerve

Immediately after exiting the intervertebral foramen, the short spinal nerve trunk divides into two main branches, or rami:

  1. Dorsal (Posterior) Ramus: This smaller ramus turns posteriorly to innervate the:

* Intrinsic (epaxial) muscles of the back (e.g., erector spinae).

* Skin overlying the back in a segmental pattern.

  1. Ventral (Anterior) Ramus: This is the larger of the two rami. It runs anterolaterally to supply the:

* Muscles (hypaxial) and skin of the anterolateral trunk and limbs.

* Formation of Plexuses: In most regions (cervical, brachial, lumbar, sacral), the ventral rami do not run independently. Instead, they merge, branch, and recombine to form complex nerve networks called plexuses.

* Cervical Plexus (C1-C4): Innervates the neck.

* Brachial Plexus (C5-T1): Innervates the upper limb.

* Lumbar Plexus (L1-L4): Innervates the anterior and medial thigh.

* Sacral Plexus (L4-S4): Innervates the posterior thigh, leg, and foot.

* In the thoracic region (T2-T12), the ventral rami remain segmental and run as the intercostal nerves.

Applied Anatomy

Lesions affecting a spinal nerve or its roots produce characteristic clinical signs and symptoms.

* Radiculopathy (Nerve Root Compression): This is commonly caused by a herniated intervertebral disc or osteophytes from degenerative joint disease. Compression of a spinal nerve root leads to:

* Pain (radicular pain): Sharp, shooting pain that radiates along the distribution of the affected nerve (e.g., sciatica from L5/S1 compression).

* Paresthesia: Numbness and tingling in the corresponding dermatome (area of skin supplied by a single spinal nerve).

* Muscle Weakness: Weakness in the muscles supplied by that nerve root (myotome).

* Diminished Reflexes: The stretch reflex arc involving the compressed nerve may be hypoactive or absent.

* Herpes Zoster (Shingles): The Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV), which causes chickenpox, can lie dormant for years in the dorsal root ganglia. Upon reactivation, it travels down the sensory nerve fibers to the skin, causing a painful, vesicular rash that is characteristically limited to a single unilateral dermatome.

* Traumatic Injury: Direct trauma, avulsion injuries (e.g., in brachial plexus injuries), or fractures of the vertebral column can damage spinal nerves or their roots, leading to a combination of motor and sensory deficits corresponding to the level of injury.

1. Define a spinal segment.

A spinal segment is the portion of the spinal cord that gives rise to a single pair of spinal nerves.

Each segment of the spinal cord is functionally and anatomically defined by the emergence of its corresponding pair of spinal nerves (one on each side). There are typically 31 spinal segments, corresponding to the 31 pairs of spinal nerves: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 1 coccygeal. The dorsal (sensory) and ventral (motor) rootlets arising from each segment unite to form a single spinal nerve.

2. Draw and label part of a multipolar neuron.

Multipolar Neuron: Labeled Structures

A multipolar neuron is the most common type of neuron, characterized by a single axon and multiple dendrites extending from the cell body.

* Cell Body (Soma/Perikaryon): The metabolic center of the neuron. It contains the nucleus and essential organelles.

* Nucleus: Contains the genetic material and controls the cell's activities.

* Nissl Bodies: These are granules of rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) and free ribosomes, responsible for protein synthesis. They are found in the cell body and dendrites, but are absent from the axon hillock.

* Dendrites: These are short, highly branched processes that extend from the cell body. They are the primary receptive sites of the neuron, responsible for receiving signals from other neurons and conducting them towards the cell body.

* Axon Hillock: A specialized, cone-shaped region of the cell body where the axon originates. It is the site where action potentials are typically initiated.

* Axon: A single, long, slender process that transmits nerve impulses (action potentials) away from the cell body to other neurons, muscles, or glands.

* Myelin Sheath: A lipid-rich, insulating layer that covers the axons of many neurons.

* It is formed by Schwann cells in the Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) and Oligodendrocytes in the Central Nervous System (CNS).

* Its function is to increase the speed of nerve impulse conduction.

* Node of Ranvier: Gaps in the myelin sheath that occur at regular intervals along the axon. Action potentials "jump" from one node to the next in a process called saltatory conduction, which greatly accelerates signal transmission.

* Axon Terminals (Synaptic Boutons): The branched endings of an axon. They contain synaptic vesicles filled with neurotransmitters and form synapses with other cells to transmit the signal.

3. Give any four differences between axon and dendrite.
FeatureAxonDendrite
Direction of ImpulseTransmits nerve impulses away from the cell body (efferent process).Receives signals and transmits them towards the cell body (afferent process).
Number and BranchingTypically a single, long process per neuron, with uniform diameter and fewer, perpendicular branches (collaterals).Usually multiple, short, highly branching processes that taper as they extend from the cell body.
MyelinationCan be covered by a myelin sheath, formed by Oligodendrocytes (CNS) or Schwann cells (PNS).Generally unmyelinated and lack myelin sheaths.
Terminal StructureEnds in specialized axon terminals (synaptic boutons) which release neurotransmitters into the synapse.Lacks specialized terminal structures for neurotransmitter release, primarily receiving signals.
4. Types (classification) of neurons.

Neurons, the structural and functional units of the nervous system, can be classified based on their structure (morphology) and their function.

I. Structural Classification

This classification is based on the number of processes (axons and dendrites) that extend from the neuron's cell body (soma).

  1. Multipolar Neurons:

* Structure: These neurons have more than two processes: one axon and multiple dendrites.

* Prevalence: They are the most common type of neuron in the human body.

* Examples: Most neurons within the Central Nervous System (CNS) are multipolar, including all motor (efferent) neurons and interneurons.

  1. Bipolar Neurons:

* Structure: They have two distinct processes extending from opposite ends of the cell body: one axon and one dendrite.

* Prevalence: Bipolar neurons are relatively rare and function as specialized sensory neurons.

* Examples: They are found in special sensory organs such as the retina of the eye, the olfactory epithelium of the nose, and in the inner ear.

  1. Unipolar (Pseudounipolar) Neurons:

* Structure: These neurons have a single, short process that emerges from the cell body and divides in a T-shape. This single process then functions as both an axon and a dendrite.

* Prevalence: They are primarily found functioning as sensory neurons.

* Examples: The majority of sensory (afferent) neurons have their cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglia of the spinal nerves and are pseudounipolar.

II. Functional Classification

This classification is based on the direction in which the nerve impulse is transmitted relative to the CNS.

  1. Sensory (Afferent) Neurons:

* Function: They transmit nerve impulses from sensory receptors in the periphery TO the Central Nervous System. The term "afferent" means carrying towards.

* Structure: Most sensory neurons are structurally unipolar (pseudounipolar).

* Location: Their cell bodies are typically located in ganglia within the Peripheral Nervous System (PNS).

  1. Motor (Efferent) Neurons:

* Function: They transmit nerve impulses FROM the Central Nervous System to effector organs, such as muscles and glands. The term "efferent" means carrying away.

* Structure: Motor neurons are structurally multipolar.

* Location: Their cell bodies are located within the CNS (e.g., in the anterior horns of the spinal cord's gray matter).

  1. Interneurons (Association Neurons):

* Function: These neurons are located entirely within the CNS and lie between sensory and motor neurons in neural pathways. Their primary role is to integrate information.

* Prevalence: They are the most abundant neurons, accounting for over 99% of all neurons in the body.

* Structure: Interneurons are almost all structurally multipolar.

5. Name any two types of synapses and two neurotransmitters.

Types of Synapses

  1. Chemical Synapse: This is the most common type of synapse, specialized for transmitting signals via chemical messengers called neurotransmitters. An action potential arriving at the presynaptic terminal triggers the release of neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft, which then bind to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, causing excitation or inhibition.
  2. Electrical Synapse: These synapses allow direct current flow between neurons through gap junctions. Gap junctions form channels that connect the cytoplasm of two cells, enabling rapid, bidirectional transmission of electrical signals without the involvement of neurotransmitters.

Neurotransmitters

  1. Acetylcholine (ACh): This neurotransmitter is released by all preganglionic neurons in both the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems. It is also released by all postganglionic parasympathetic neurons and by postganglionic sympathetic neurons innervating sweat glands. It primarily acts on nicotinic and muscarinic receptors.
  2. Norepinephrine (NE): Also known as noradrenaline, this neurotransmitter is released by most postganglionic sympathetic neurons. It mediates the "fight or flight" responses of the sympathetic nervous system by acting on adrenergic receptors on target organs.
6. Mention the types of neuroglia with examples.

Neuroglia, or glial cells, are non-excitable support cells of the nervous system. They are far more numerous than neurons and are categorized based on their location within the nervous system:

* CNS Glia: These glial cells are found within the Central Nervous System (brain and spinal cord).

* Astrocytes: Star-shaped cells that are the most abundant. They provide structural support to neurons, form the blood-brain barrier (BBB), and regulate the chemical environment of the CNS.

* Oligodendrocytes: These cells form myelin sheaths around axons in the CNS, increasing the speed of nerve impulse conduction.

* Microglia: These are phagocytic cells that act as the immune defense system of the CNS, removing debris and pathogens.

* Ependymal Cells: These cells line the ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord, and are involved in the production and circulation of Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF).

* PNS Glia: These glial cells are located in the Peripheral Nervous System.

* Schwann Cells: These cells form myelin sheaths around axons in the PNS, similar to oligodendrocytes in the CNS, and play a crucial role in nerve regeneration after injury.

* Satellite Cells: These cells surround the neuron cell bodies within PNS ganglia, providing structural support and regulating the chemical environment around the neurons.

1. Describe the female mammary gland under the following headings: (a) Extent/position, (b) Structure, (c) Relations, (d) Blood supply, (e) Lymphatic drainage, (f) Nerve supply, (g) Applied anatomy, and (h) Development.

(a) Extent/Position

The mammary gland is a modified sweat gland located within the superficial fascia of the pectoral region. Its typical extent is from the 2nd to the 6th ribs vertically, and from the sternal margin medially to the mid-axillary line laterally. A significant extension of glandular tissue, known as the Axillary Tail of Spence, passes through the foramen of Langer in the deep fascia and extends into the axilla, which is clinically important for tumor metastasis.

(b) Structure

The breast consists of the nipple, areola, and internal glandular and stromal components. The nipple is a conical projection containing circularly arranged smooth muscle fibers (for erection) and 15-20 lactiferous duct openings. The areola is the pigmented skin surrounding the nipple, housing sebaceous glands (Montgomery's tubercles) which lubricate the nipple during lactation. Internally, the breast is organized into 15-20 lobes arranged radially, each drained by a lactiferous duct. These lobes are subdivided into lobules, which contain the milk-producing alveoli. The supporting framework, or stroma, is composed of fibrous connective tissue and abundant adipose tissue, which largely determines the breast's size and shape. Fibrous septa, known as suspensory ligaments of Cooper, extend from the deep layer of superficial fascia through the glandular tissue to attach to the deep surface of the skin, providing support.

(c) Relations

The mammary gland lies in the superficial fascia superficial to the deep pectoral fascia. It rests primarily on the pectoralis major, serratus anterior, and partially on the external oblique muscles. A crucial anatomical relation is the retromammary space, a loose areolar tissue plane situated between the deep surface of the breast and the deep pectoral fascia. This space allows for breast mobility on the chest wall and is often exploited during mastectomy.

(d) Blood Supply

The arterial supply to the mammary gland is rich, primarily sourced from:

  1. Internal thoracic artery: Via its perforating branches (especially 2nd-4th intercostal spaces), which supply the medial part of the breast.
  2. Lateral thoracic artery: A branch of the axillary artery, supplying the lateral part of the breast with lateral mammary branches.
  3. Thoracoacromial artery: Specifically its pectoral branch, contributing to the superior aspect.
  4. Posterior intercostal arteries: The 2nd-4th posterior intercostal arteries provide lateral cutaneous branches that supply the lateral and posterior parts of the breast.

Venous drainage generally mirrors the arterial supply, primarily to the axillary vein (superficial veins) and internal thoracic vein (deep veins), with some contribution to intercostal veins.

(e) Lymphatic Drainage

The lymphatic drainage of the breast is of paramount clinical importance, especially concerning breast cancer metastasis. Lymphatics originate from a subcutaneous plexus and the glandular tissue, coalescing into the subareolar lymphatic plexus (of Sappey). From here, three major pathways exist:

* Axillary Lymph Nodes (75%): This is the predominant route, draining mainly the lateral quadrants. Axillary nodes are categorized into Level I (lateral to pectoralis minor, including anterior/pectoral, posterior/subscapular, and lateral groups), Level II (deep to pectoralis minor, including central and interpectoral/Rotter's nodes), and Level III (medial to pectoralis minor, the apical group). Lymph typically flows from Level I to II to III, then to the supraclavicular nodes and eventually into the subclavian lymphatic trunk.

* Parasternal (Internal Mammary) Lymph Nodes (20%): These nodes lie along the internal thoracic vessels and primarily drain the medial quadrants of the breast.

* Posterior Intercostal Lymph Nodes (5%): These drain the deepest parts of the breast and can facilitate spread to the vertebral column or pleura.

(f) Nerve Supply

The mammary gland receives its nerve supply mainly from the anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the 4th to 6th intercostal nerves. These provide sensory innervation to the skin of the breast and the nipple-areola complex. Autonomic fibers also supply the smooth muscle of the nipple and the blood vessels within the breast tissue.

(g) Applied Anatomy

Several clinical conditions are directly linked to the anatomy of the female mammary gland:

* Breast Cancer: The most common cancer in females, frequently metastasizing via the lymphatic routes, especially to axillary lymph nodes.

* Peau d'Orange: An "orange peel" appearance of the skin, caused by obstruction of superficial lymphatics by cancer cells, leading to edema and pitting around hair follicles.

* Nipple Retraction: Inward pulling of the nipple, often due to shortening or fibrosis of lactiferous ducts secondary to tumor infiltration.

* Skin Dimpling: Localized indentation of the skin, resulting from cancer infiltrating and shortening the suspensory ligaments of Cooper.

* Polymastia: Presence of accessory breasts, typically along the embryonic milk line (axilla to groin).

* Polythelia: Presence of accessory nipples without glandular tissue, also along the milk line.

* Mastitis: Inflammation of breast tissue, common during lactation, usually due to bacterial infection entering via nipple cracks.

* Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy: A crucial procedure to identify and remove the first draining lymph node(s) to assess cancer spread, guiding further surgical management.

(h) Development

The mammary glands develop from paired mammary ridges, or milk lines, which are ectodermal thickenings extending from the axilla to the groin in the 4th week of embryonic development. Normally, only the pectoral portion of these ridges persists. From this persistent ectoderm, mammary buds proliferate and grow into the underlying mesenchyme, forming solid cords that canalize to become rudimentary lactiferous ducts by birth. In prepubertal females and males, the gland remains rudimentary. At puberty, under the influence of estrogen, the duct system elongates and branches, while progesterone stimulates the development of glandular alveoli within the lobules. This process involves significant fat deposition, contributing to breast enlargement. Anomalies like polymastia and polythelia occur due to the failure of complete regression of parts of the embryonic milk line.

1. Retromammary space.

Definition

The retromammary space is a potential space located deep to the mammary gland. It is not an actual open space but rather a region filled with loose areolar connective tissue.

Location

It lies between the deep surface of the breast and the deep pectoral fascia, which covers the pectoralis major muscle. Superiorly, it is continuous with the superficial fascia of the neck, and inferiorly with the superficial fascia of the abdomen.

Composition

This space is primarily composed of loose areolar tissue, which is a type of connective tissue characterized by its sparse arrangement of fibers and abundant ground substance. This allows for relative ease of movement between the structures it separates.

Function

The primary function of the retromammary space is to provide mobility for the breast over the underlying deep pectoral fascia and muscles. This allows the breast to move freely during arm movements and physical activity.

Clinical Significance

* Breast Mobility: The presence of this loose connective tissue plane is crucial for the natural movement of the breast.

* Mastectomy: Surgeons utilize this space during a mastectomy to separate the breast tissue from the underlying chest wall muscles with relative ease. It allows for removal of the entire mammary gland while preserving the pectoralis major muscle in a modified radical mastectomy.

* Breast Implants: This space is a common site for the placement of subglandular breast implants, positioning the implant directly behind the glandular tissue but in front of the muscle.

* Tumor Invasion: While it provides mobility, extensive breast cancers can infiltrate through the deep fascia into the retromammary space and subsequently invade the underlying pectoralis major muscle, indicating a more advanced stage of disease. This can also cause fixation of the breast to the chest wall.

* Infections/Abscesses: Although less common, infections or abscesses can form within this space.

2. Peau d'orange.

Peau d'Orange

Peau d'orange is a distinctive clinical sign observed in the breast, characterized by a dimpled, pitted appearance of the skin, akin to the texture of an orange peel. It is predominantly seen in cases of advanced breast cancer.

The pathological basis for this phenomenon is the obstruction of the superficial lymphatics within the dermal layer of the breast skin by infiltrating cancer cells. This lymphatic blockage leads to an accumulation of fluid, causing edema (swelling) of the skin. The sweat gland orifices and hair follicles, however, are tethered to deeper structures by fibrous septa (including the suspensory ligaments of Cooper). As the surrounding edematous tissue swells, these tethered points remain depressed, resulting in the characteristic pitted and "orange peel" appearance.

Its clinical significance is paramount, as peau d'orange is a classic indicator of locally advanced breast cancer, often implying a more aggressive disease with involvement of the dermal lymphatics. This finding typically correlates with a less favorable prognosis.

3. Clavipectoral fascia.

The Clavipectoral fascia is a strong, dense fibrous sheet of deep fascia located deep to the Pectoralis Major muscle in the pectoral region. It envelops both the Subclavius and Pectoralis Minor muscles.

Attachments

* Superiorly: It splits into two layers to enclose the Subclavius muscle, with the anterior layer attaching to the anterior surface of the clavicle and the posterior layer to its posterior surface.

* Medially: It fuses with the external intercostal membrane of the first two intercostal spaces and the first rib.

* Laterally: It attaches to the coracoid process (forming the costocoracoid ligament) and merges with the deltoid fascia.

* Inferiorly: It extends downwards as the Suspensory Ligament of Axilla (Gerdy's ligament), which then fuses with the Axillary Fascia, forming the floor of the axilla.

Parts/Divisions

* Costocoracoid membrane: This is the part of the fascia situated between the Subclavius muscle superiorly and the Pectoralis Minor muscle inferiorly. Medially, it thickens to form the Costocoracoid Ligament, which extends from the first costochondral junction to the coracoid process.

* Suspensory ligament of axilla (of Gerdy): This is the inferior continuation of the fascia below the Pectoralis Minor muscle, which merges with the axillary fascia. It plays a crucial role in keeping the axillary fascia taut and maintaining the dome-shaped contour of the axilla.

Structures Piercing the Clavipectoral Fascia

Several important structures pass through openings in the clavipectoral fascia:

* Lateral Pectoral Nerve (supplying Pectoralis Major)

* Cephalic Vein (draining into the axillary vein)

* Thoracoacromial Artery (and its branches, including pectoral, deltoid, acromial, and clavicular)

* Lymphatics (connecting infraclavicular nodes to axillary nodes)

Associated Structures & Clinical Significance

* Deltopectoral Triangle (Clavipectoral Triangle): This triangular depression is bounded superiorly by the clavicle, medially by the Pectoralis Major, and laterally by the Deltoid. The Cephalic Vein runs within this groove before piercing the clavipectoral fascia to drain into the axillary vein. The deltoid branch of the thoracoacromial artery also runs here.

* Surgical Landmark: The clavipectoral fascia is an important anatomical landmark for surgeons operating in the axilla or anterior chest wall due to its consistent attachments and the structures it transmits.

* Infections: Its fascial planes can guide the spread of infections or contain abscesses in the subpectoral space.

* Axillary Support: The suspensory ligament of the axilla is essential for maintaining the integrity and shape of the axillary floor, and its damage or laxity can contribute to drooping of the axilla.

4. Structures piercing clavipectoral fascia.

Introduction to the Clavipectoral Fascia

The clavipectoral fascia is a strong sheet of deep fascia located in the pectoral region, deep to the clavicular head of the pectoralis major muscle. It encloses the subclavius and pectoralis minor muscles. The part of the fascia extending between the subclavius and pectoralis minor is known as the costocoracoid membrane, and it is this section that is pierced by several important neurovascular structures.

Structures Piercing the Clavipectoral Fascia

Four key structures pierce the clavipectoral fascia, typically superior to the pectoralis minor muscle. A useful mnemonic to remember these is CALT: Cephalic vein, Acromiothoracic artery (thoracoacromial artery), Lateral pectoral nerve, and Tributaries (Lymphatics).

  1. Cephalic Vein:

* This large superficial vein of the upper limb ascends in the deltopectoral groove.

* It pierces the clavipectoral fascia in the deltopectoral triangle to drain into the axillary vein. It is the only structure that pierces the fascia to enter the deeper axillary space from a superficial position.

  1. Thoracoacromial Artery (Acomiothoracic Artery):

* A short trunk arising from the second part of the axillary artery.

* It pierces the costocoracoid membrane and immediately divides into its four terminal branches: Pectoral, Acromial, Clavicular, and Deltoid ("PDAC"). These branches supply the surrounding muscles and bones.

  1. Lateral Pectoral Nerve:

* Arises from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus (C5, C6, C7).

* It pierces the fascia to provide motor innervation primarily to the pectoralis major muscle. A communicating branch often loops to join the medial pectoral nerve.

  1. Lymphatics:

* Lymphatic vessels from the pectoral region and breast, particularly from the infraclavicular nodes, pierce the fascia to drain into the apical group of axillary lymph nodes. This pathway is significant for the metastasis of breast cancer.

5. Winging of scapula and how it is produced.

Winging of Scapula (Scapula Alata)

Description:

Winging of the scapula, also known as Scapula Alata, is a characteristic clinical deformity where the medial border and inferior angle of the scapula protrude posteriorly. This occurs because the scapula loses its normal stabilization and can no longer be held firmly against the thoracic wall. The protrusion becomes especially noticeable when the patient pushes against a wall with outstretched arms or attempts to abduct the arm.

Production Mechanism:

The winging of the scapula is primarily caused by dysfunction of the Serratus Anterior muscle, which is crucial for holding the scapula against the chest wall and rotating it during abduction. This dysfunction typically arises from damage to its nerve supply, the Long Thoracic Nerve. The mechanism unfolds as follows:

  1. Damage to Long Thoracic Nerve: The Long Thoracic Nerve (of Bell), originating directly from the roots of the brachial plexus (C5, C6, C7), innervates the Serratus Anterior muscle. It runs superficially on the muscle and is susceptible to injury from various causes, including trauma (e.g., direct blow to the lateral chest, stretch injuries), surgical procedures (e.g., mastectomy, axillary lymph node dissection), or prolonged pressure (e.g., carrying heavy backpacks), as well as inflammatory conditions.
  2. Paralysis of Serratus Anterior Muscle: Damage to the Long Thoracic Nerve leads to paralysis or paresis of the Serratus Anterior muscle, compromising its ability to contract and perform its actions.
  3. Loss of Scapular Stabilization: With a paralyzed Serratus Anterior, the muscle can no longer effectively hold the scapula firmly against the thoracic wall. The scapula loses its key stabilizing force, and its ability to protract and upwardly rotate is severely impaired.
  4. Posterior Protrusion (Winging): Consequently, the unopposed actions of other muscles, combined with gravity and movements of the arm, cause the medial border and inferior angle of the scapula to detach and protrude posteriorly and medially away from the rib cage, creating the characteristic "winged" appearance. This makes it difficult or impossible to perform actions like pushing, punching, or abducting the arm above 90 degrees due to inadequate upward rotation of the glenoid cavity.

1. Mammary gland—blood supply, lymphatic drainage and applied anatomy.

Blood Supply and Venous Drainage

The mammary gland has a rich arterial supply from multiple sources, ensuring adequate blood flow for lactation.

Arterial Supply:

* Internal Thoracic Artery: Perforating branches, particularly from the 2nd to 4th intercostal spaces, supply the medial aspects of the breast (medial mammary branches).

* Lateral Thoracic Artery: A branch of the second part of the axillary artery, it runs along the lateral border of the pectoralis minor and provides lateral mammary branches to the superolateral part of the breast.

* Thoracoacromial Artery: The pectoral branch of this artery, which arises from the second part of the axillary artery, contributes to the supply.

* Posterior Intercostal Arteries: Lateral cutaneous branches from the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th posterior intercostal arteries supply the posterolateral aspect of the gland.

Venous Drainage:

The veins generally follow the arteries and drain into three main systems:

  1. Axillary Vein: Receives the majority of the drainage, primarily from the lateral aspect of the breast via the lateral thoracic vein.
  2. Internal Thoracic Vein: Drains the medial aspect of the breast.
  3. Posterior Intercostal Veins: Provide a minor drainage pathway that connects to the azygos system of veins.

Lymphatic Drainage

The lymphatic drainage of the breast is of immense clinical importance, as it is the primary route for the metastasis of breast cancer. Lymph from the breast parenchyma drains to the subareolar plexus of Sappey.

Primary Drainage Pathways:

* Axillary Lymph Nodes (Approx. 75%): This is the main drainage route, especially for the lateral quadrants and the axillary tail of Spence. The nodes are clinically divided into three levels based on their relation to the pectoralis minor muscle:

* Level I: Nodes lateral to the pectoralis minor (Anterior/Pectoral, Posterior/Subscapular, and Lateral groups).

* Level II: Nodes deep to the pectoralis minor (Central group and interpectoral/Rotter's nodes).

* Level III: Nodes medial to the pectoralis minor (Apical group).

Lymph flows sequentially from Level I → Level II → Level III, then to the supraclavicular nodes and into the subclavian lymphatic trunk.

* Parasternal (Internal Mammary) Lymph Nodes (Approx. 20%): These nodes lie along the internal thoracic vessels and primarily drain the medial quadrants of the breast. This pathway can lead to spread to the mediastinum or the contralateral breast.

* Posterior Intercostal Lymph Nodes (Approx. 5%): Drains the deep, posterior parts of the breast and can be a route for metastasis to the vertebrae or pleura.

Applied Anatomy

* Breast Cancer: The most common cancer in females. Malignant tumors, typically arising from ductal or lobular epithelium, metastasize primarily via the lymphatic system. Axillary lymph node status is the single most important prognostic factor.

* Peau d'Orange ("Orange Peel" Skin): This sign is caused by obstruction of superficial lymphatics by cancer cells. The resulting lymphedema causes the skin to become thick and pitted around hair follicles.

* Skin Dimpling: Infiltration and shortening of the suspensory ligaments of Cooper by an underlying tumor pulls the skin inward, creating a visible indentation or pucker.

* Nipple Retraction: An inward pulling or inversion of the nipple, which can be a sign of malignancy. It is caused by the infiltration and subsequent fibrotic shortening of the lactiferous ducts by a tumor.

* Mastitis: Inflammation of the breast tissue, most commonly seen in lactating women. It is typically caused by a bacterial infection (e.g., *Staphylococcus aureus*) entering through a crack in the nipple.

* Polymastia and Polythelia: The presence of an accessory breast or an accessory nipple, respectively. These developmental anomalies occur along the embryonic milk line, which extends from the axilla to the groin.

2. Pectoralis major.

Introduction

Pectoralis major is a large, fan-shaped muscle that forms the bulk of the anterior chest wall, connecting the upper limb to the trunk. It is composed of a clavicular head and a larger sternocostal head.

Origin

* Clavicular Head: Arises from the anterior surface of the medial half of the clavicle.

* Sternocostal Head: Arises from the anterior surface of the sternum, the cartilages of the 2nd to 6th ribs, and the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle.

Insertion

The muscle inserts via a broad, bilaminar (U-shaped) tendon into the lateral lip of the bicipital (intertubercular) groove of the humerus. The sternocostal fibers twist behind the clavicular fibers to insert more superiorly on the humerus.

Nerve Supply

The muscle has a dual nerve supply from the brachial plexus:

* Lateral Pectoral Nerve (C5, C6, C7): Primarily supplies the clavicular head.

* Medial Pectoral Nerve (C8, T1): Pierces pectoralis minor to supply the sternocostal head.

Blood Supply

* Pectoral branch of the thoracoacromial artery.

* Perforating branches from the internal thoracic artery.

* Branches from the lateral thoracic artery.

Actions

* Adduction and Medial Rotation: Powerful adductor and medial rotator of the arm.

* Flexion: The clavicular head flexes the arm at the shoulder joint.

* Extension: The sternocostal head extends the flexed arm against resistance (e.g., pulling up).

* Accessory Muscle of Inspiration: When the arm is fixed, it elevates the rib cage during forced inspiration.

Clinical Significance

* Poland Syndrome: A congenital condition characterized by the unilateral absence or hypoplasia of the pectoralis major muscle, often associated with ipsilateral syndactyly.

* Surgical Flaps: The muscle is commonly used as a pedicled flap for reconstruction in head, neck, and chest wall surgery.

* Mastectomy: In a radical mastectomy, the pectoralis major is removed. In a modified radical mastectomy, which is more common today, the muscle is preserved to maintain arm function and chest wall contour.

3. Pectoralis minor.

Pectoralis Minor

Pectoralis minor is a small, triangular muscle situated deep to the pectoralis major in the anterior chest wall.

* Origin: Anterior surfaces of the 3rd, 4th, and 5th ribs near their costal cartilages.

* Insertion: Medial border and superior surface of the coracoid process of the scapula.

* Nerve Supply: Medial pectoral nerve (C8, T1), which pierces it to also supply the sternocostal head of pectoralis major.

* Blood Supply: Primarily from the pectoral branch of the thoracoacromial artery and branches of the lateral thoracic artery.

* Actions:

* Protraction and depression of the scapula.

* Downward rotation of the scapula, depressing the glenoid cavity.

* When the scapula is fixed, it acts as an accessory muscle of inspiration by elevating ribs 3-5.

Clinical Significance

Pectoralis minor is a crucial surgical and anatomical landmark. It divides the axillary artery and axillary lymph nodes into three distinct parts for descriptive and clinical purposes.

* Level I Axillary Nodes: Lateral to the muscle.

* Level II Axillary Nodes: Deep/posterior to the muscle.

* Level III Axillary Nodes: Medial to the muscle.

Hypertrophy or spasm of the muscle can compress the underlying brachial plexus and axillary artery against the thoracic wall, contributing to Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (TOS).

4. Clavipectoral fascia—extent, attachments and structures piercing it.

Introduction and Extent

The clavipectoral fascia is a strong, fibrous sheet of deep fascia located deep to the clavicular head of the pectoralis major muscle. It serves to invest two key muscles of the pectoral region and helps form the anterior wall of the axilla.

Its extent can be described in parts:

* Superiorly, it splits to enclose the subclavius muscle.

* The portion between the subclavius and pectoralis minor muscles is known as the costocoracoid membrane.

* Inferiorly, it encloses the pectoralis minor muscle.

* Below the pectoralis minor, it continues downwards as the suspensory ligament of the axilla (of Gerdy), which attaches to and supports the dome of the axillary fascia, creating the hollow of the armpit.

Attachments

The clavipectoral fascia has the following attachments:

* Superiorly: It attaches to the clavicle, splitting to enclose the subclavius muscle.

* Inferiorly: It is continuous with the axillary fascia via the suspensory ligament of the axilla.

* Medially: It fuses with the first rib, its costal cartilage, and the external intercostal membrane of the upper two intercostal spaces.

* Laterally: It attaches to the coracoid process of the scapula and blends with the coracoclavicular ligament.

Structures Piercing the Clavipectoral Fascia

Four key structures pierce the costocoracoid membrane portion of the clavipectoral fascia. These are:

* Cephalic vein: Ascends in the deltopectoral groove and pierces the fascia to drain into the axillary vein.

* Thoracoacromial artery: A branch of the second part of the axillary artery, it pierces the fascia and divides into its pectoral, acromial, clavicular, and deltoid (P.D.A.C.) branches.

* Lateral pectoral nerve: Arises from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus and pierces the fascia to supply the pectoralis major muscle.

* Lymphatics: Lymph vessels passing from the infraclavicular lymph nodes to the apical group of axillary lymph nodes.

5. Serratus anterior—attachments, nerve supply and actions.

Origin

The Serratus Anterior is a large, sheet-like muscle that originates from the outer surfaces of the upper 8 or 9 ribs via a series of muscular slips. The first slip arises from both the 1st and 2nd ribs.

Insertion

The muscle inserts onto the anterior (costal) surface of the medial border of the scapula:

* Upper slips (from ribs 1-2) insert onto the superior angle.

* Middle slips (from ribs 2-3) insert along the medial border.

* Lower slips (from ribs 4-9), the most powerful part, converge to insert on the inferior angle.

Nerve Supply

The Serratus Anterior is innervated by the Long Thoracic Nerve of Bell, which arises directly from the roots of the brachial plexus (C5, C6, C7). The nerve runs on the superficial surface of the muscle, making it vulnerable to injury.

Actions

  1. Protraction of the Scapula: It pulls the scapula forward and laterally around the thoracic wall. This is the primary muscle for pushing and punching actions, earning it the nickname "boxer's muscle".
  2. Upward Rotation of the Scapula: The lower slips pull the inferior angle of the scapula laterally and forward, which is essential for abducting the arm above 90 degrees.
  3. Stabilization: It holds the scapula firmly against the thoracic wall.
  4. Accessory Muscle of Respiration: When the scapula is fixed, it can elevate the ribs to aid in forced inspiration.

Clinical Significance

Paralysis of the Serratus Anterior due to injury of the Long Thoracic Nerve results in a condition called "Winging of the Scapula". In this condition, the medial border and inferior angle of the scapula protrude posteriorly, especially when the patient pushes against a wall.

1. Describe the root value, formation, course, relations and branches of axillary nerve. Give its applied anatomy. What are the effects of injury at surgical neck of humerus?

Root Value and Formation

The axillary nerve is a major nerve of the upper limb that arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus. Its root value is from the ventral rami of the C5 and C6 spinal nerves.

Course and Relations

The axillary nerve originates in the axilla, posterior to the axillary artery. It courses inferiorly and laterally, exiting the axilla by passing through the quadrangular space.

* Quadrangular Space Boundaries:

* Superior: Teres minor muscle.

* Inferior: Teres major muscle.

* Medial: Long head of the triceps brachii muscle.

* Lateral: Surgical neck of the humerus.

* Contents of the Quadrangular Space: The axillary nerve passes through this space accompanied by the posterior circumflex humeral artery and vein.

After passing through the quadrangular space, the nerve winds around the surgical neck of the humerus deep to the deltoid muscle. Here, it divides into its terminal branches.

Branches

The axillary nerve provides motor, sensory, and articular branches:

  1. Articular Branch: Before dividing, it gives a branch to the capsule of the glenohumeral (shoulder) joint.
  2. Anterior Branch: This branch winds around the surgical neck of the humerus and supplies the anterior and middle parts of the deltoid muscle. It terminates as the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm, which supplies sensory innervation to the skin over the lower part of the deltoid (the "regimental badge" area).
  3. Posterior Branch: This branch supplies the teres minor muscle and the posterior part of the deltoid muscle. It may also give off a small cutaneous branch.

Applied Anatomy

The axillary nerve is clinically significant due to its vulnerability to injury at two main sites:

* Anterior dislocation of the shoulder joint: The head of the humerus can stretch or compress the nerve as it is displaced inferiorly and anteriorly.

* Fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus: The nerve's close proximity to the bone at this location makes it susceptible to damage during fractures.

Effects of Injury at the Surgical Neck of Humerus

Injury to the axillary nerve at the surgical neck of the humerus results in a combination of motor and sensory deficits:

* Motor Effects:

* Paralysis of the deltoid muscle leads to a loss of the rounded contour of the shoulder, resulting in a flattened appearance. Over time, this leads to significant deltoid atrophy.

* The primary action affected is abduction of the arm at the shoulder joint. While the supraspinatus can initiate the first 15 degrees, the deltoid is the prime mover from 15 to 90 degrees. Therefore, the patient will have profound weakness in abducting the arm beyond 15 degrees.

* Paralysis of the teres minor muscle results in weakness of lateral (external) rotation of the arm.

* Sensory Effects:

* There is a loss of sensation in the skin over the lower half of the deltoid muscle, an area often referred to as the "regimental badge area." This is due to damage to the terminal upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm.

1. Nerve supply and action of deltoid.

Deltoid Muscle

The deltoid is a large, triangular muscle that covers the shoulder joint, giving the shoulder its characteristic rounded contour.

Nerve Supply

* Axillary Nerve (C5, C6): The deltoid muscle is innervated by the axillary nerve, a terminal branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus.

* Course: The nerve exits the axilla by passing through the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral artery. It then winds around the surgical neck of the humerus, making it vulnerable to injury in this location.

Actions

The deltoid muscle has three distinct sets of fibers, each with a primary action.

  1. Anterior (Clavicular) Fibers: Responsible for flexion and medial rotation of the arm at the glenohumeral joint.
  2. Middle (Acromial) Fibers: The most powerful part of the muscle and the prime mover of arm abduction from 15° to 90°. It takes over from the supraspinatus, which initiates the first 15° of abduction.
  3. Posterior (Spinal) Fibers: Responsible for extension and lateral rotation of the arm.

All fibers work together to stabilize the glenohumeral joint and prevent inferior dislocation of the humeral head.

Clinical Correlation

Injury to the axillary nerve, commonly due to a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus or an anterior dislocation of the shoulder joint, results in paralysis of the deltoid muscle. This leads to:

* Loss of shoulder contour, resulting in a flattened appearance.

* Inability to abduct the arm beyond 15 degrees.

* Sensory loss over the "regimental badge" area on the lateral aspect of the shoulder, which is supplied by the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm (a branch of the axillary nerve).

2. Rotator cuff (muscles forming it).

The rotator cuff is a functional musculotendinous unit that surrounds the glenohumeral (shoulder) joint. It is composed of four scapulohumeral muscles whose tendons blend with the fibrous capsule of the joint, forming a "cuff" that provides dynamic stability and facilitates a wide range of arm movements.

Muscles of the Rotator Cuff (SITS)

The four muscles are best remembered by the mnemonic SITS.

MuscleOriginInsertion (on Humerus)Main Action(s)Nerve Supply
SupraspinatusSupraspinous fossa of scapulaSuperior facet of Greater TubercleInitiates abduction of the arm (the first 15°)Suprascapular nerve (C5, C6)
InfraspinatusInfraspinous fossa of scapulaMiddle facet of Greater TubercleLateral (external) rotation of the armSuprascapular nerve (C5, C6)
Teres MinorUpper 2/3rds of lateral border of scapulaInferior facet of Greater TubercleLateral (external) rotation of the armAxillary nerve (C5, C6)
SubscapularisSubscapular fossa of scapulaLesser TubercleMedial (internal) rotation of the arm; powerful adductorUpper & Lower Subscapular nerves (C5, C6)

Collective Function

The primary function of the rotator cuff as a unit is to provide dynamic stability to the highly mobile but inherently unstable glenohumeral joint. During arm movements, these muscles contract to depress and centralize the humeral head within the shallow glenoid fossa, preventing its superior or anterior displacement. This synergistic action allows for smooth rotation and abduction of the humerus.

Clinical Relevance

* Rotator Cuff Tears: This is a common shoulder injury, often due to overuse, trauma, or age-related degeneration. The supraspinatus tendon is the most frequently torn, as it passes through the subacromial space where it can be impinged by the acromion. This results in shoulder pain, weakness, and a characteristic "painful arc" of motion during abduction (typically between 60-120°).

* Shoulder Dislocation: The rotator cuff is the main dynamic stabilizer preventing dislocation. Weakness or traumatic failure of these muscles significantly increases the risk of the humeral head dislocating from the glenoid fossa, most commonly in an anterior direction.

3. Boundaries and contents of the inferior triangular intermuscular space in the arm.

The inferior triangular intermuscular space, also known as the triangular interval, is a space in the posterior arm and scapular region that allows passage of key neurovascular structures from the axilla to the posterior arm.

Boundaries

* Superior: Inferior border of the Teres Major muscle.

* Medial: Lateral border of the long head of the Triceps Brachii muscle.

* Lateral: Shaft of the Humerus.

Contents

The following structures pass through the triangular interval to enter the posterior compartment of the arm:

* Radial nerve (C5-T1)

* Profunda Brachii artery (deep artery of the arm), which is the largest branch of the brachial artery.

4. Axillary nerve in relation to surgical neck of humerus.

Origin

The axillary nerve is a terminal branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus, containing nerve fibers from the C5 and C6 spinal roots.

Course and Relation to Surgical Neck of Humerus

The axillary nerve exits the axilla posteriorly by passing through the quadrangular space. It then winds intimately around the surgical neck of the humerus, making it highly susceptible to injury at this location.

* Quadrangular Space Boundaries:

* Superior: Teres minor muscle

* Inferior: Teres major muscle

* Medial: Long head of the triceps brachii

* Lateral: Surgical neck of the humerus

* Accompanying Vessel: Throughout its course around the humerus, the axillary nerve is accompanied by the posterior circumflex humeral artery.

Innervation

* Motor Supply: The axillary nerve provides motor innervation to the deltoid and teres minor muscles.

* Sensory Supply: It provides cutaneous sensation to the skin over the lower part of the deltoid muscle, an area known as the "regimental badge" area, via the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm.

Clinical Correlation

Due to its close anatomical relationship, the axillary nerve is commonly injured in fractures of the surgical neck of the humerus or during anterior dislocation of the shoulder joint.

* Motor Deficits: Paralysis of the deltoid muscle leads to a loss of the rounded contour of the shoulder and an inability to abduct the arm beyond the initial 15 degrees (which is initiated by the supraspinatus). Paralysis of teres minor results in weakness of lateral rotation.

* Sensory Deficits: A characteristic loss of sensation is found over the "regimental badge" area on the lateral aspect of the shoulder.

1. Deltoid muscle—location, attachments, nerve supply and action.

Location

The Deltoid muscle is a large, triangular muscle that covers the shoulder joint, giving the shoulder its characteristic rounded contour. It is located superficially, extending from the shoulder girdle to the humerus.

Attachments

Origin

The deltoid muscle originates from a broad area:

* The lateral one-third of the clavicle.

* The acromion of the scapula.

* The spine of the scapula.

Insertion

All fibers of the deltoid converge to insert onto the deltoid tuberosity on the lateral aspect of the shaft of the humerus.

Nerve Supply

The deltoid muscle is innervated by the Axillary nerve (fibers from C5, C6 spinal nerves), which is a branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus.

Actions

The actions of the deltoid muscle vary based on its different fiber segments:

* Middle fibers: These are the prime mover for abduction of the arm (after the initial 15 degrees, which is initiated by the supraspinatus).

* Anterior fibers: Contribute to flexion and medial rotation of the arm at the glenohumeral joint.

* Posterior fibers: Contribute to extension and lateral rotation of the arm at the glenohumeral joint.

2. Structures under cover of deltoid muscle.

The deltoid muscle, a large, triangular muscle that gives the shoulder its rounded contour, covers several crucial anatomical structures. Originating from the lateral one-third of the clavicle, the acromion, and the spine of the scapula, and inserting onto the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus, it forms a protective cover for the glenohumeral joint and associated neurovascular elements.

Structures Under Cover of the Deltoid Muscle

* Muscles:

* Rotator Cuff Muscles (SITS): All four muscles – Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres Minor, and Subscapularis – along with their respective tendons, lie deep to the deltoid. These tendons insert onto the greater and lesser tubercles of the humerus.

* Teres Major: The superior part of this muscle, which lies inferior to Teres Minor, is also partially covered.

* Long head of Biceps Brachii tendon: This tendon traverses the intertubercular groove of the humerus, held in place by the transverse humeral ligament, and is an intra-capsular structure deep to the deltoid.

* Nerves:

* Axillary nerve (C5, C6): This nerve, responsible for motor innervation of the deltoid and teres minor, exits the axilla through the quadrangular space. It then winds around the surgical neck of the humerus deep to the deltoid, where it is vulnerable to injury. It also provides cutaneous sensation via the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm.

* Vessels:

* Posterior Circumflex Humeral Artery: This artery closely accompanies the axillary nerve through the quadrangular space and supplies the deltoid and surrounding structures, coursing deep to the deltoid around the surgical neck of the humerus.

* Joint Structures & Bursae:

* Glenohumeral (Shoulder) Joint Capsule: The fibrous capsule of the shoulder joint, along with its reinforcing ligaments (glenohumeral and coracohumeral ligaments), is directly deep to the deltoid muscle.

* Subacromial/Subdeltoid Bursa: This large bursa lies between the deltoid (and acromion/coracoacromial arch) superiorly and the joint capsule/supraspinatus tendon inferiorly, reducing friction during shoulder movements.

* Surgical Neck of Humerus: This region of the humerus, including the greater and lesser tubercles (sites of rotator cuff insertion), is covered by the deltoid.

The intricate arrangement of these structures highlights the complexity of the shoulder joint and the protective role the deltoid muscle plays, while also making it a key landmark for accessing deeper components.

3. Rotator cuff of shoulder.

The rotator cuff is a critical group of four muscles that encircle the glenohumeral joint of the shoulder. These muscles, along with their tendons, blend with the joint capsule to form a "cuff" around the head of the humerus, providing vital dynamic stability and facilitating a wide range of movements of the arm.

Rotator Cuff Muscles (SITS)

The four muscles of the rotator cuff are often remembered by the mnemonic SITS:

MuscleOriginInsertion (on Humerus)Main ActionNerve Supply
SupraspinatusSupraspinous fossa of scapulaSuperior facet of Greater TubercleInitiates abduction (first 15°)Suprascapular nerve (C5, C6)
InfraspinatusInfraspinous fossa of scapulaMiddle facet of Greater TubercleLateral rotation of armSuprascapular nerve (C5, C6)
Teres MinorUpper 2/3rds of lateral border of scapulaInferior facet of Greater TubercleLateral rotation of armAxillary nerve (C5, C6)
SubscapularisSubscapular fossa of scapulaLesser TubercleMedial rotation of armUpper and Lower Subscapular nerves (C5, C6)

Function

The primary function of the rotator cuff muscles is to stabilize the head of the humerus within the shallow glenoid cavity of the scapula. This dynamic stabilization is crucial given that the glenohumeral joint is the most mobile, yet least stable, joint in the body. In addition to stabilization, these muscles are responsible for initiating and contributing to the rotation (medial and lateral) and abduction of the humerus. The Supraspinatus is particularly notable for initiating abduction during the first 15 degrees, after which the deltoid muscle takes over as the prime mover.

Clinical Relevance

* Rotator Cuff Tears: These are common injuries, particularly in overhead athletes and older individuals. The Supraspinatus tendon is the most frequently torn due to its position, making it susceptible to impingement as it passes under the acromion. Tears can lead to shoulder pain, weakness in abduction and rotation, and restricted movement.

* Shoulder Impingement Syndrome: This occurs when the rotator cuff tendons (especially supraspinatus) and bursa become compressed beneath the acromion during arm elevation, leading to pain and inflammation.

* Shoulder Dislocation: Healthy and strong rotator cuff muscles are vital in preventing glenohumeral joint dislocations, particularly anterior dislocations, by keeping the humeral head firmly seated in the glenoid fossa.

4. Describe the boundaries and contents of the intermuscular spaces in the upper limb (quadrangular and triangular spaces).
